title: How Suicide Bombers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how suicide bombing works and its history, opening with Josh's reaction to a CNN segment that celebrated a Libyan rebel who blew himself up in a car bomb. They trace martyrdom from the Book of Daniel (Nebuchadnezzar and the fiery furnace) and the Masada standoff, through jihad in the Quran and the Crusades, to the Hashashin assassins, Kamikaze pilots, and the 1983 Beirut embassy and Marine barracks bombings. They cover the typical profile of bombers (often ages 18 to 24, grieving personal loss, oppression), recruitment and handlers who keep bombers committed, the 2011 Moscow cell phone spam text incident, the cost and explosives used (such as TNT and TATP), the human shield effect on blast zones, and the dehumanization that fuels cycles of violence. The episode ends with a thank-you in place of listener mail and a promo for the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
topics: Moscow Red Square cell phone spam text bombing

segments.title: Opening banter and CNN segment
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter, then Josh describes a CNN segment about the family of a Libyan man who blew himself up in a car bomb, and says the coverage read like state TV celebrating a suicide bomber.

segments.title: Martyrdom origins
segments.summary: They define martyrdom as sacrificing one's life for a cause, often with a reward in the afterlife, and trace its roots to the Book of Daniel story of Nebuchadnezzar and the fiery furnace, which Chuck suggests may be a parable about torture.

segments.title: Masada and jihad
segments.summary: They mention the Masada standoff, where rebels killed themselves rather than surrender to Rome, and then discuss the rise of Islam and the two parts of jihad, the inner struggle and the physical battle.

segments.title: Crusades and Hashashin assassins
segments.summary: They describe the Crusades as a Christian holy war, and explain that the word assassin derives from the Hashashin, a radical Shiite sect that killed public officials in public places before the Mongols wiped them out in 1257.

segments.title: Kamikaze and the modern suicide attack
segments.summary: They compare Kamikaze pilots in World War Two to suicide bombers, then cite the 1983 suicide truck bombing of the U.S. embassy in Beirut and the Marine barracks bombing that followed as the start of the modern suicide attack.

segments.title: Profile of suicide bombers and recruitment
segments.summary: They discuss the typical bomber, often aged 18 to 24, who feels despondent and oppressed and often has lost family members, and how handlers and supporters isolate and encourage recruits, including martyrdom videos. A Moscow New Year's Eve case is covered where a would-be bomber was killed when a provider's spam text triggered her phone.
topics: Moscow cell phone spam text bombing

segments.title: How the bombs are built and blast effects
segments.summary: They explain that a suicide bomb is cheap and simple, with materials ranging from re-jiggered land mines to TNT and TATP, delivered by vests, belts, bags, cars, trucks, or boats. A crowd around the bomber acts as a human shield that increases the blast zone. They also mention the 2005 London shooting of an innocent Brazilian man.

segments.title: Goals of attacks and dehumanization
segments.summary: They outline three goals of suicide attacks: terror, attention to a cause, and morale effects. They discuss how Reagan withdrew from Lebanon after the Marine bombing, and how dehumanizing each side fuels the conflict, including a proposal to bury bombers in pigskin.

segments.title: Thank-you and sign-off
segments.summary: In place of listener mail, Josh and Chuck thank listeners, invite emails, and promote the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
topics: Stuff from the Future video podcast
